live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL (Kimsuky): a North Korea-attributed espionage group that mixes phishing, fake installers and mobile…
next.in_short: Vendors and South Korean agencies attribute NICKEL KIMBALL, better known as Kimsuky, to North Korea. It has been tied to spear-phishing, trojanized installers, ClickFix lures and Android spyware, mostly aimed at South Korea.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as NICKEL KIMBALL. The catalogue lists many aliases, including Kimsuky, APT43, THALLIUM, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, Springtail and Black Banshee.
Symantec describes Springtail, also called Kimsuky, as a North Korean espionage group. It writes that the U.S. government has said the group is a unit of North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau.
Microsoft, as reported by BleepingComputer, calls Kimsuky a North Korean state actor.
Sekoia and Kudelski Security note that some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster with several branches, such as TA406 and TA408. They add that vendors divide and name clusters differently.
Genians says some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group. It cites the MSMT report, which assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.

South Korea's National Police Agency says Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023. The flaw allowed large files to be downloaded without authentication.
Microsoft says its limited attacks since January 2025 hit people in international affairs organizations, NGOs, government agencies and media companies.
AhnLab reported signs in July 2022 that AppleSeed, a backdoor it says Kimsuky mainly uses, was being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit.

South Korean officials said hackers believed to be operating from North Korea breached the nuclear research body KAERI through a VPN flaw. One of the IP addresses involved was linked to infrastructure used by Kimsuky.

AhnLab says Kimsuky spreads the PebbleDash backdoor mainly through spear-phishing. The emails carry shortcut (LNK) files disguised as documents, and the chain uses PowerShell and Dropbox. AhnLab says PebbleDash was once tied to Lazarus.

Microsoft says Kimsuky has adopted ClickFix-style tactics. A fake South Korean official builds contact with the target, then tells them to run attacker code in PowerShell. The code installs a browser-based remote desktop tool.

Breakglass Intelligence attributes a three-stage chain to Kimsuky with high confidence. It starts from a CHM help file and ends in a keylogger with clipboard monitoring. The report maps about 79 domains, including Naver-themed lures for South Korean users.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new DOCSWAP Android variants to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean comments. The apps pose as delivery apps and carry a RAT with 57 commands. ENKI calls this strong evidence, not definitive confirmation.

Symantec reports that Springtail built Linux.Gomir, a Linux version of the GoBear backdoor. It links the group to Troll Stealer, delivered in Trojanized software installers aimed largely at South Korean targets.

A January 2021 article citing ESTsecurity says Thallium altered the installer of a private stock investment messaging app. The researchers said it was unclear whether the aim was money or spying on traders.
South Korea's NCSC says Kimsuky compromised a construction trade website in January 2024. It used the site to push trojanized security installers signed with a valid certificate.

Genians assesses with moderate confidence that a 2026 campaign using NodeLinkRAT was Kimsuky's work. It began with reply-based spearphishing posing as a National Assembly aide. Genians says a third party imitating the same techniques cannot be ruled out.
Treat unexpected replies, shortcut files disguised as documents and requests to paste commands into PowerShell with suspicion, even when the sender seems to be a known official.
Install software only from verified sources, and keep VPN and email servers patched.
